blocks.text: A man in his sixties, three days after bowel surgery, vomits and has a swollen abdomen. His abdominal film shows a ladder of gas-filled loops stacked across the centre of the film. Before any scan, a trained eye can often tell you where the blockage is from the gas alone.

blocks.markdown: Plain films work because tissues attenuate X-rays differently: gas appears black, fat dark grey, soft tissue and fluid mid grey, bone and calcium white. In the abdomen the gas inside the bowel outlines the lumen, so the **pattern of gas** is the main thing you read. Normally gas sits mostly in the stomach and colon, with a little in the small bowel.

blocks.title: Bowel gas pattern
blocks.text: The distribution, calibre and wall markings of gas within the gastrointestinal lumen on an abdominal radiograph. Small bowel is central and shows valvulae conniventes (folds that cross the full width of the lumen); large bowel is peripheral and shows haustra (folds that cross only part of the width).

rows: Valvulae conniventes cross the whole lumen
Haustra cross only part of the lumen
blocks.caption: Distinguishing small from large bowel on a supine abdominal film. Limits are widely taught guides and vary slightly between sources.

blocks.markdown: Obstruction causes proximal dilatation because gas and fluid cannot pass the blockage. **Small bowel obstruction** is commonly due to adhesions (from previous surgery), an incarcerated hernia, or a tumour. **Large bowel obstruction** is commonly due to colorectal carcinoma, a sigmoid or caecal volvulus, or a diverticular stricture. Gas is absent or reduced distal to the block, so the level of the transition from dilated to collapsed bowel localises the obstruction.
Radiographs magnify structures lying away from the detector. If the true diameter is $d$, the measured diameter on the film is larger by the magnification factor $M$:

blocks.caption: Correcting a measured bowel diameter for magnification (M is stated for the film or estimated from a marker of known size).

blocks.title: Correcting a bowel measurement
blocks.prompt: A loop of small bowel measures 3.6 cm on a supine film with a known magnification factor of 1.2. Is it dilated?

steps.text: Write the correction formula: the film overstates the size, so divide the film measurement by $M$.
Compare with the upper limit for small bowel (3 cm): the loop is at the limit, so it is not clearly dilated once magnification is allowed for.

blocks.answer: True diameter 3.0 cm: borderline, not clearly dilated.

blocks.markdown: Fractures are described with a fixed vocabulary so that anyone reading the report can picture the film. State, in order: **site** (which bone; proximal, middle or distal third of a long bone, or diaphysis, metaphysis, epiphysis; whether it enters a joint), **pattern** (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, segmental, greenstick in a child, avulsion), and **displacement** (translation of the distal fragment relative to the proximal one, angulation, rotation, shortening). Also state whether the skin is intact (closed) or broken (open).

blocks.title: Describe the distal fragment
blocks.text: Displacement and angulation are always described as the position of the distal fragment relative to the proximal fragment, and the apex of angulation is named by the direction it points (for example apex anterior).

blocks.title: Describing a fracture
blocks.prompt: An adult film of the forearm shows a break through the middle third of the radial shaft. The line runs across the shaft at about 90 degrees to its long axis. The distal fragment lies half a shaft width towards the ulna, with no angulation, and the skin is intact. Write the description.

steps.text: Site: radius, middle third of the diaphysis, not intra-articular.
Pattern: the line runs at about 90 degrees to the long axis, so it is transverse; there is one line only, so it is not comminuted.
Displacement: the distal fragment is translated by half a shaft width towards the ulna (50% translation), with no angulation.

blocks.answer: Closed, transverse fracture of the mid-shaft radius with 50% translation of the distal fragment towards the ulna and no angulation.

blocks.markdown: Landmarks give you the frame for reading bone films. In the **spine** on an anteroposterior (AP) view you see vertebral bodies, the pedicles seen end-on as oval outlines, and the midline spinous processes, which should lie centred between the pedicles; on a lateral view you follow the smooth lines of the anterior and posterior vertebral body margins. In the **proximal femur** identify the head, neck, greater trochanter (lateral) and lesser trochanter (medial, posterior). In the **upper limb** note the olecranon of the ulna, the radial head and the scaphoid in the wrist. A smooth curve, **Shenton's line**, runs along the inferior border of the superior pubic ramus and the medial border of the femoral neck; a break in it suggests a fracture or dislocation.

items: Check the film is correctly labelled and covers the whole area, with two views at right angles.
Follow each cortex as a continuous line; step-offs and lucent lines suggest fracture.
Check alignment and joint congruity, then soft tissues for swelling or gas.
Describe site, pattern and displacement in that order.

blocks.title: Two views and the joint above and below
blocks.text: A single view can hide displacement. Always obtain two views at right angles and include the joints above and below a long bone fracture; an abdominal film showing dilated loops also needs correlation with the clinical picture, as gas pattern alone does not prove the cause.

points: Small bowel is central with valvulae conniventes crossing the full width; large bowel is peripheral with haustra crossing part of the width.
Obstruction produces proximal dilatation (3 cm small bowel, 6 cm colon, 9 cm caecum as guides) with collapse distally; causes include adhesions, hernia, carcinoma and volvulus.
Describe fractures by site, pattern and displacement of the distal fragment relative to the proximal, and state open or closed.
Know the main landmarks: vertebral pedicles and spinous processes, femoral neck and trochanters, Shenton's line.

questions.stem: A supine abdominal film shows dilated loops lying centrally, with fine folds that run across the full width of each loop. Which segment of bowel is most likely dilated?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: complete folds (valvulae conniventes) in central loops identify small bowel.
distractorRationale.b: The sigmoid has haustra or no folds and lies in the pelvis, not centrally.
distractorRationale.c: The caecum lies in the right iliac fossa and shows haustra, not full-width folds.
distractorRationale.d: The transverse colon is peripheral/anterior and shows incomplete haustral folds.

questions.explanation: Valvulae conniventes cross the whole lumen of the small bowel, whereas haustra cross only part of the lumen in the colon. Central position plus full-width folds therefore points to small bowel.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with a long history of abdominal surgery has vomiting and colicky pain. The film shows several dilated central loops with no gas in the rectum. Which cause is most likely?

options.text: Normal gas pattern in a thin patient

distractorRationale.a: Correct: adhesions are the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction after previous surgery.
distractorRationale.b: Haustral markings are a normal colonic feature, not a cause of obstruction.
distractorRationale.c: Normal patients do not have multiple dilated loops with absent distal gas.
distractorRationale.d: Vertebral compression does not obstruct the bowel.

questions.explanation: Dilated small bowel with absent distal gas indicates obstruction, and adhesions after earlier operations are the most common cause. Hernias and tumours are the other leading causes, but the surgical history makes adhesions most likely.

questions.stem: A film shows a large gas-filled loop of bowel shaped like a coffee bean, arising from the pelvis and pointing toward the right upper quadrant, with proximal colonic dilatation. This best fits which cause of large bowel obstruction?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a massively dilated twisted sigmoid loop gives this coffee-bean shape.
distractorRationale.b: Adhesions produce dilated central small bowel, not a single large peripheral loop.
distractorRationale.c: Gallstone ileus gives small bowel obstruction, often with gas in the biliary tree.
distractorRationale.d: Faecal loading shows faecal mottling, not a single twisted loop.

questions.explanation: A twisted sigmoid colon fills with gas into a single giant loop that rises out of the pelvis. It is a classic cause of large bowel obstruction, whereas adhesions and gallstone ileus cause small bowel obstruction.

questions.stem: A loop of ascending colon measures 7.2 cm in width on an abdominal film whose magnification factor is 1.2. Using $d_{\text{true}} = d_{\text{film}}/M$, calculate the true diameter in cm.
questions.explanation: True diameter = 7.2 divided by 1.2 = 6.0 cm. This is at the upper limit of normal for the large bowel, so it is not dilated by the 6 cm guide; failing to correct for magnification would have overcalled it.

questions.stem: A radiograph of the tibia shows a break running obliquely and spiralling around the shaft, with two additional small fragments. Which terms best describe the pattern?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a spiral line with extra fragments is spiral and comminuted.
distractorRationale.b: A transverse line is at right angles to the shaft, not spiralling.
distractorRationale.c: Greenstick fractures are incomplete and occur in children.
distractorRationale.d: Avulsion is a fragment pulled off at a tendon or ligament attachment.

questions.explanation: Pattern describes the line of the fracture, and the presence of more than two fragments is called comminution. A spiral line with extra fragments is therefore a comminuted spiral fracture.

questions.stem: A mid-shaft femoral fracture is imaged. The shaft is 30 mm wide. The distal fragment is translated 12 mm medially relative to the proximal fragment. Express the translation as a percentage of shaft width.
questions.explanation: Translation as a fraction of shaft width is 12/30 = 0.40, which is 40%. Describing it relative to shaft width lets readers compare films regardless of patient size or magnification.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how displacement is reported?

options.text: As the position of the distal fragment relative to the proximal fragment
As the position of the proximal fragment relative to the distal fragment
As the position of the joint above the fracture
As the direction of the X-ray beam

questions.correctOptionText: As the position of the distal fragment relative to the proximal fragment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the distal fragment is described relative to the proximal one.
distractorRationale.b: The proximal fragment is taken as the fixed reference, not the other way round.
distractorRationale.c: The joint is not the reference for displacement.
distractorRationale.d: Beam direction defines the view, not the displacement.

questions.explanation: By convention the proximal fragment is treated as the reference and the distal fragment is described relative to it. This keeps reports consistent between readers.

questions.stem: On an AP film of the lumbar spine, which pair of structures can be identified as oval rings seen end-on and the midline projections that should sit between them?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pedicles appear as ovals on the AP view and the spinous process lies centrally between them.
distractorRationale.b: Ribs are not part of the lumbar spine and transverse processes project laterally.
distractorRationale.c: Psoas margins are soft-tissue lines, not a bony landmark pair.
distractorRationale.d: Sacral ala are part of the sacrum, not paired with vertebral bodies in this way.

questions.explanation: On an AP film the pedicles are seen end-on as oval outlines on either side of the vertebral body, and the spinous process projects centrally between them. A spinous process displaced to one side may indicate rotation or a unilateral problem.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old footballer falls and has a painful wrist. List the landmarks and checks you would use to read the wrist and forearm films, and explain why two views are needed.
markingGuide: Name bones to be checked: distal radius, ulna, scaphoid and other carpal bones.
Follow each cortex for continuity, noting lucent lines or step-offs.
Two views at right angles needed because displacement may only be visible on one.
questions.explanation: A systematic approach (label, bones, cortex, alignment, soft tissue) avoids missed injuries. A single view is a flat projection, so a fracture running in the beam direction or a displaced fragment can be invisible without an orthogonal view.

questions.stem: Explain why the level of transition between dilated and collapsed bowel helps localise an obstruction, and name two common causes of obstruction of the small bowel and two of the large bowel.
markingGuide: Proximal to the block, gas and fluid accumulate and the bowel dilates.
Distal to the block, bowel is collapsed or empty of gas.
The transition point therefore marks the level of obstruction.
Small bowel causes: adhesions, hernia, tumour (any two).
Large bowel causes: carcinoma, volvulus, diverticular stricture (any two).
questions.explanation: Content that cannot pass the blockage accumulates above it and the segment beyond is empty. Reading the transition and the bowel type (small or large) therefore narrows the differential causes.
